doc_description: U.S. SEC Annual Report on Form 10-K for NIKE, Inc. for FY2023 (year ended May 31, 2023), detailing the world’s largest athletic brand’s NIKE, Jordan and Converse operations; NIKE Direct and wholesale channels; globally outsourced manufacturing concentrated in Vietnam/Indonesia/China; geographic segments (North America, EMEA, Greater China, APLA); FY23 results ($51.2B revenue amid margin pressure); principal risks, properties and leadership; and a new $18B share repurchase program.

structure.title: Preface
structure.summary:
- NIKE, Inc.’s Annual Report on Form 10-K for the fiscal year ended May 31, 2023, filed with the U.S. SEC (Commission File No. 1-10635), identifying NIKE as an Oregon corporation with principal offices in Beaverton, OR.
- Cover-page disclosures: NYSE-listed Class B common stock (ticker NKE); Class A and Class B share counts; market value of non-affiliate holdings; registrant status as a well-known seasoned issuer and large accelerated filer; confirmation of periodic filing compliance, interactive data submission, and auditor attestation of internal control over financial reporting; not a shell company; documents incorporated by reference (2023 Proxy Statement for Part III).
- Table of Contents outlining Parts I–IV, including Item 1 (Business), Item 1A (Risk Factors), Item 7 (MD&A), Item 8 (Financial Statements), and other standard 10-K items.
- Item 1. Business — General: NIKE’s core activities are the design, development, and worldwide marketing and sale of athletic footwear, apparel, equipment, accessories, and services. Products are sold via NIKE Direct (owned retail stores and digital platforms), wholesale to retail accounts, and through distributors, licensees, and sales reps globally. Nearly all products are manufactured by independent contractors, with most footwear and apparel made outside the U.S.; equipment is made both domestically and abroad. NIKE is the largest seller of athletic footwear and apparel globally.
- Item 1. Business — Products: NIKE Brand offerings organized around Men’s, Women’s, and Kids’, plus Jordan Brand and Converse. Emphasis on innovation and high-quality construction. Footwear and apparel designed primarily for athletic use but also worn casually; leading sales in Men’s and Women’s categories and Jordan footwear. Apparel marketed in collections and includes licensed college and professional team/league products. Equipment and accessories include bags, socks, balls, eyewear, timepieces, digital devices, bats, gloves, and protective gear. Subsidiary NIKE IHM (Air Manufacturing Innovation) sells plastic products to other manufacturers. Jordan Brand focuses on basketball performance and culture (results reported within NIKE Brand geographies). Converse designs and licenses casual sneakers, apparel, and accessories (reported standalone). NIKE also licenses third parties to make and sell certain apparel, digital devices/apps, and sports equipment using NIKE-owned trademarks.

structure.start_phrase: NIKE, Inc. was incorporated in 1967 under the laws of the State of Oregon.
structure.summary:
- Overview of NIKE, Inc.: Incorporated in Oregon in 1967; largest global seller of athletic footwear and apparel; terminology for references in the Annual Report.
- Core business: Design, development, worldwide marketing and sales of athletic footwear, apparel, equipment, accessories, and services.
- Go-to-market model: NIKE Direct (owned retail stores and NIKE Brand Digital), wholesale to retail accounts, and distribution via independent distributors, licensees, and sales reps across nearly all countries; provision of interactive digital consumer services and experiences.
- Manufacturing: Predominantly by independent contractors; most footwear and apparel made outside the U.S.; equipment made both in the U.S. and abroad.
- Fiscal year convention: Fiscal years end on May 31 (e.g., fiscal 2023 ended May 31, 2023).
- Product alignment: NIKE Brand organized around Men’s, Women’s, and Kids’; additional focus on Jordan Brand and Converse to meet consumer needs and drive growth.
- Footwear: Designed primarily for sport but widely worn casually; strong emphasis on innovation and quality; Men’s, Women’s, and Jordan Brand lead in footwear sales.
- Apparel: Sports apparel mirrors footwear strategy (innovation, quality, athletic-to-casual use); marketed in collections and includes licensed college/professional team and league logos; Men’s and Women’s lead in apparel sales.
- Equipment and accessories: NIKE-branded bags, socks, balls, eyewear, watches, digital devices, bats, gloves, protective gear, and other sport equipment; NIKE IHM, Inc. (Air Manufacturing Innovation) produces plastic products for other manufacturers.
- Jordan Brand: Designs, distributes, and licenses basketball-focused footwear, apparel, and accessories under the Jumpman; results reported within NIKE Brand geographic segments.
- Converse: Wholly owned, Boston-based brand designing, distributing, and licensing casual sneakers, apparel, and accessories under Converse-related trademarks; results reported on a stand-alone basis.
- Licensing: Agreements with unaffiliated parties to manufacture and sell certain apparel, digital devices/apps, and sports equipment using NIKE-owned trademarks.

structure.summary:
- Overview: NIKE, Inc., incorporated in Oregon in 1967, is the world’s largest seller of athletic footwear and apparel. It designs, develops, markets, and sells footwear, apparel, equipment, accessories, and services globally through NIKE Direct (owned retail and digital) and wholesale channels. Most products are made by independent contractors, with nearly all footwear and apparel produced outside the U.S. Equipment is made both domestically and abroad. Fiscal years end May 31.

- Product portfolio: Organized around Men’s, Women’s, and Kids’, plus Jordan Brand and Converse. Emphasis on innovation and high-quality construction. Footwear and apparel are designed for sport but widely worn casually; leading sales in Men’s, Women’s, and Jordan footwear, and Men’s and Women’s apparel. Also sells performance equipment and accessories (e.g., bags, socks, balls, eyewear, devices, protective gear) and produces plastic components via NIKE IHM (Air Manufacturing Innovation). - Brand structure: Jordan Brand focuses on basketball performance and culture (reported within NIKE Brand geographic segments). Converse is a wholly-owned subsidiary with its own trademarks (e.g., Chuck Taylor, All Star) and is reported as a separate operating segment.

- Sales and marketing dynamics: Moderate seasonal fluctuations with Q1 and Q4 typically higher than Q2 and Q3; product mix varies by season and geography. Demand is influenced by sport popularity, fitness trends, and design shifts; NIKE invests in marketing and rapid product adaptation to mitigate related risks.

- Geographic reporting: NIKE Brand segments are North America, EMEA, Greater China, and APLA; NIKE Direct results are managed within each geography. Converse operates as its own reportable segment, including digital commerce.

- U.S. market specifics: U.S. sales for NIKE Brand and Converse represented ~43% of total FY23 revenue (up from 40% in FY22 and 39% in FY21). Products are sold through a broad mix of retail accounts; the three largest U.S. customers comprised ~22% of U.S. sales in FY23. Direct-to-consumer presence includes digital platforms and 369 U.S. stores (213 NIKE factory, 74 NIKE in-line including employee-only, 82 Converse). NIKE operates eight significant U.S. distribution centers.

Product innovation leverages market intelligence and technologies including Nike Air, Zoom, Free, Dri-FIT, Flyknit, FlyEase, ZoomX, Air Max, React, and Forward.

- Manufacturing and supply chain footprint: Nearly all footwear and apparel are produced by independent contract manufacturers. As of May 31, 2023, there were 146 strategic Tier 2 material suppliers.
  - Footwear: 123 finished-goods factories in 11 countries; 15 contract manufacturers. FY23 production by country: Vietnam ~50%, Indonesia ~27%, China ~18%. Four manufacturers each produced >10% of footwear; collectively ~58%. Largest single factory ~9%.

- International operations and trade environment: Exposure to risks from changing trade policies, tariffs, anti-dumping, quotas, sanctions, capital controls, and geopolitical instability. Protectionist measures have increased product costs and could adversely affect sales/profitability. NIKE monitors and engages in administrative/judicial processes, advocates for trade liberalization, and works with industry coalitions. The company believes it can develop alternative supply sources over time if needed, though short-term disruptions and higher ongoing costs may occur.

structure.title: International Operations and Trade
structure.heading: International Operations and Trade
structure.start_phrase: Our international operations and sources of supply are subject to the usual risks of doing business abroad, such as the implementation of, or potential changes in, foreign and domestic trade policies, increases in import duties, anti-dumping measures, quotas, safeguard measures, trade restrictions, restrictions on the transfer of funds and, in certain parts of the world, political tensions, instability, conflicts, nationalism and terrorism, and resulting sanctions and other measures imposed in response to such issues.
structure.summary:
- Manufacturing and sourcing: Concentration of apparel production among contract manufacturers (one >10%; top five ~52%); contractors source most raw materials locally. Key footwear materials include rubbers, plastics, foams, leathers, textiles, and polyurethane films for Air-Sole components. Air-Sole supply from NIKE’s Air Manufacturing Innovation (facilities in Oregon, Missouri, Vietnam) and contract manufacturers in China and Vietnam.
- Apparel materials: Use of natural/synthetic fabrics, recycled content, specialized performance textiles (moisture-wicking, thermal, weather-repellent), and hardware.
- Supply chain in fiscal 2023: Early-year volatility that improved over time; higher network costs from inflation; sufficient raw material availability despite competition; sourcing risks referenced to Risk Factors.
- Financing partner: Since 1972, Sojitz Corporation of America provides import-export financing and holds NIKE’s redeemable preferred stock.
- International operations and trade risks: Exposure to changing trade policies, tariffs, anti-dumping, quotas, trade restrictions, fund transfer limits, and geopolitical tensions/sanctions. Rising global protectionism has increased product costs; NIKE monitors, litigates/advocates to mitigate restrictions and supports trade liberalization. Ability to shift sourcing over time, though alternatives may be less cost-effective and temporarily disruptive.
- Compliance: Operations subject to the U.S. FCPA and other anti-bribery laws; NIKE maintains an ethics and compliance program for employees, agents, suppliers, and partners.
- Competition: Highly competitive global market with major rivals (e.g., adidas, Anta, ASICS, Li Ning, lululemon, New Balance, Puma, Under Armour, V.F.). NIKE is the largest seller; key competitive factors include product quality/innovation/design/price-value, consumer engagement and endorsements/digital experience, and effective sourcing, distribution, and merchandising.
- Intellectual property: Trademarks (including NIKE and Swoosh registered in 190+ jurisdictions), trade dress rights, copyrights, and extensive U.S./foreign utility and design patents covering technologies, designs, manufacturing, and digital products/software. NIKE pursues registrations strategically and vigorously enforces IP; success relies on design, R&D, production, and marketing supported by IP protection.

structure.title: Competition
structure.heading: Competition

structure.summary:
- International operations compliance: Emphasis on adherence to the U.S. Foreign Corrupt Practices Act and other anti-bribery laws; significant sourcing and consumer markets outside the U.S.; existence of an ethics and compliance program for employees, agents, suppliers, and partners; reference to Item 1A Risk Factors for related risks.
- Competitive landscape: The global athletic footwear, apparel, and equipment market is highly competitive and fast-changing; key competitors include adidas, Anta, ASICS, Li Ning, lululemon, New Balance, Puma, Under Armour, and V.F. Corporation; NIKE states it is the largest seller in the category; competition centers on product quality, performance, design, innovation, price/value; consumer engagement via marketing, digital experiences, social media, customer service, endorsements (athletes, influencers, teams, leagues), and events; effective sourcing, distribution, and merchandising (in-store and digital) are critical; references to related risk factors.
- Intellectual property strategy: IP is central to brand strength and competitiveness; extensive use and global registration of trademarks, including NIKE and the Swoosh in 190+ jurisdictions; ownership of additional trademarks and trade dress rights for distinctive shoe designs (some registered); copyrights in designs, graphics, software, digital goods, and other works; broad portfolio of U.S. and foreign utility and design patents covering components, technologies, materials, manufacturing techniques, features, industrial designs, equipment, digital devices, and related software, with varying expiration dates; success tied to capabilities in design, R&D, production, and marketing supported by IP; ongoing strategy to apply for/register IP in the U.S. and select foreign countries and to vigorously enforce against infringement and misappropriation.

structure.title: Trademarks and Patents
structure.heading: Trademarks and Patents
structure.start_phrase: We believe that our intellectual property rights are important to our brand, our success and our competitive position.
structure.summary:
- Compliance: Emphasis on adhering to the U.S. Foreign Corrupt Practices Act and other anti-bribery laws across global operations. Nike sources heavily and sells internationally, and maintains an ethics and compliance program covering employees, agents, suppliers, and partners. References to Risk Factors for international risks.
- Competition: The athletic footwear, apparel, and equipment market is intensely competitive and rapidly changing. Nike competes globally with adidas, Anta, ASICS, Li Ning, lululemon, New Balance, Puma, Under Armour, and V.F. Corporation, among others. Nike states it is the largest seller worldwide. Key competitive factors include:
  - Product quality, performance, reliability, innovation, design, and price/value.
  - Brand connection via marketing, digital experiences, social media, customer service, endorsements by athletes/influencers/teams/leagues, and sponsored events/clinics.
  - Effective sourcing, distribution, merchandising, and presentation in-store and online.
- Intellectual Property: IP is central to brand and competitive position. Nike:
  - Uses and registers trademarks broadly, with NIKE and the Swoosh registered in 190+ jurisdictions; holds additional marks and trade dress rights (some registered).
  - Holds copyrights in designs, graphics, software applications, digital goods, and other original works.
  - Owns numerous U.S. and foreign utility and design patents covering components, technologies, materials, manufacturing techniques, features, functionality, industrial designs, and related software for footwear, apparel, equipment, and digital devices; patents expire at various times.
  - Attributes success to capabilities in design, R&D, production, and marketing, supported by IP rights, and follows a policy of applying for and registering IP in the U.S. and select foreign countries, vigorously enforcing against infringement and misappropriation.

structure.title: Human Capital Resources
structure.heading: Human Capital Resources
structure.start_phrase: At NIKE, we consider the strength and effective management of our workforce to be essential to the ongoing success of our business.
structure.summary:
- Focus on human capital as a key driver of business success, emphasizing attraction, development, and retention of a diverse, engaged workforce that fuels creativity and innovation.
- Culture anchored by NIKE’s Maxims and Code of Conduct; mission to bring inspiration and innovation to every athlete; commitment to employee growth via training on company values, leadership development, managerial tools, and tuition reimbursement.
- Regular employee engagement surveys and pulse checks assessing satisfaction, emotional commitment, and DE&I culture; multiple speak-up channels for reporting concerns.
- Community impact goal to invest 2% of prior fiscal year pre-tax income in initiatives, primarily to get kids active through sport and to advance equity; employee giving and volunteer efforts matched by the NIKE Foundation.
- Workforce profile: approximately 83,700 employees as of May 31, 2023, plus contractors and temporary personnel.
- Labor relations: some employees in EMEA and APLA represented by trade unions and/or works councils per local law; compliance with industry/national collective bargaining in certain European countries; no material operational disruptions from labor disputes.
- DE&I as a strategic priority with fiscal 2025 targets to increase representation of women globally and U.S. racial/ethnic minorities (including Director+ levels); recruiting through diverse partnerships and institutions, DE&I education for leaders and teams, and employee networks (NikeUNITED).
- Broader DE&I impact through community investments and business diversity efforts, including training programs for women and increased use of minority-owned suppliers.
- Competitive, equitable total rewards: annual pay and promotion reviews; company-wide and retail bonus plans tied to performance; comprehensive family care benefits; military leave; access to Sport Centers; mindfulness and mental health resources (EAP and counseling); crisis support (including COVID-19 and disasters).
- Flexible work: hybrid model, Four Week Flex (up to four weeks working from any location annually), Well-Being Week (corporate office closure) and Well-Being Days for retail and distribution center teams.
- Inclusive healthcare and financial support: family planning and transgender healthcare coverage for U.S. plan participants; unlimited free financial coaching for U.S. employees.
- References to additional human capital details in the FY22 NIKE, Inc. Impact Report (website references not incorporated by reference).
- Availability of corporate governance documents and SEC filings (10-K, 10-Q, 8-K, proxies) on NIKE’s investor website and on sec.gov; documents available free of charge, with print copies via NIKE Investor Relations; website information not incorporated by reference.

- Special note on forward-looking statements: cautions about uncertainties that may cause actual results to differ; NIKE’s policy not to disclose material non-public info to analysts or confirm third-party forecasts.
- Economic and industry risks: impacts from inflation, interest rates, recession risk, discretionary consumer spending, FX volatility, commodity/raw material costs, supply chain constraints, and heightened competition across footwear, apparel, equipment, and digital services.
- Currency and inflation exposure: translation and transaction impacts, effects of hedging, and potential disruption to suppliers from FX swings.
- Wholesale customer health: credit risk, order cancellations, bankruptcies, and dependence on retailers’ merchandising and store investments.
- Climate and sustainability: physical risks from climate change and extreme weather; regulatory divergence and added compliance/reporting costs; challenges achieving sustainability targets and potential reputational impact.
- Natural disasters/extreme weather: operational disruptions to stores, suppliers, distribution centers, IT, and consumer demand.
- Public health emergencies: supply chain and logistics disruptions, factory and store closures, changing consumer traffic and demand, higher operating costs, canceled sports events, wholesale bankruptcies, and capital market volatility.
- Brand, reputation, and culture: risks from product quality, marketing, social media amplification, supplier practices, positions on social issues, and adverse publicity involving key people or partners.
- Seasonality and demand variability: quarter-to-quarter fluctuations tied to product mix, events timing, weather, and other external factors.
- Consumer preference and innovation: need to anticipate trends, deliver product innovation and quality; risk of failed launches or marketing.
- Endorsements: rising costs to attract/retain talent; reputational risks or performance issues with endorsers.
- Demand forecasting and inventory: risk of excess stock or shortages affecting margins, cash flow, and relationships.
- NIKE Direct (retail and digital): high fixed investments, lease commitments, store performance risks, fraud and theft, digital platform performance/scalability, user experience, and competitive features.
- Information technology and cybersecurity: reliance on complex global systems; risks from outages, upgrades, remote work, cyber-attacks, and financial reporting impacts.
- Licensing: dependence on licensees’ execution and brand stewardship; potential revenue impact from misuse or poor performance.
- Retailer consolidation: concentrated credit risk and reduced alternative channels if large accounts pull back.
- Financial counterparties: exposure to defaults by banks/derivative counterparties.
- Concentrated manufacturing base: reliance on a limited number of specialized footwear factories and potential supply disruptions.
- Real estate: competition for prime sites, lease renewals/modifications, and profitability management of the store fleet.
- Talent and labor: attraction/retention of key employees, cultural integrity, evolving work models, immigration shifts, and potential labor actions or changing employment regulations.
- Global operations: geopolitical conflicts, trade barriers, terrorism/war, differing regulations, and cross-border shipment delays.
- Sourcing/manufacturing/logistics: raw material availability and costs, wage/labor standards, unexpected factory closures, transportation capacity, port congestion/strikes, oil prices, and need for costly air freight; impacts from changing trade policies/tariffs.
- Distribution network: dependence on efficient operation and third-party performance; vulnerability to disasters and IT issues.
- Legal, regulatory, and compliance: broad global compliance obligations; litigation and investigations; evolving rules for virtual goods/crypto; potential sanctions and reputational harm.
- Trade policy and sanctions: tariffs, quotas, embargoes, retaliatory measures, and operational changes stemming from policy shifts; anti-corruption compliance risks.
- Intellectual property: counterfeiting, enforcement challenges, potential infringement claims, confidentiality leaks, and novel IP issues for virtual goods.
- Data privacy and security: breach risks, heightened global privacy regimes (GDPR, UK GDPR, China PIPL, US state laws), compliance costs, fines, and reputational damage.
- Tax risks: changing global tax frameworks (OECD Pillar One/Two), EU minimum tax adoption, audits/transfer pricing disputes, state aid investigations, and volatility in effective tax rate.
- Supply chain responsibility: risks from contractors’/licensees’ noncompliance with codes of conduct, labor, environmental, and product safety standards.
- Investments and liquidity: risk that major investments (e.g., NIKE Direct, tech, capacity) don’t yield expected returns; exposure to principal shareholder stock sales; credit rating changes affecting borrowing costs and access to capital.
- Internal controls and accounting estimates: potential control failures and sensitivity to critical estimates affecting reported results.
- Corporate governance/stock: anti-takeover provisions; risk of missing market expectations, stock price volatility, and related securities litigation.

structure.title: Management's Discussion and Analysis of Financial Condition and Results of Operations
structure.heading: ITEM 7. Management's Discussion and Analysis of Financial Condition and Results of Operations
structure.start_phrase: NIKE designs, develops, markets and sells athletic footwear, apparel, equipment, accessories and services worldwide.
structure.summary:
- Overview and strategy: NIKE is the world’s largest athletic footwear and apparel seller, operating through NIKE Direct (owned stores and digital), wholesale, distributors and licensees. The Consumer Direct Acceleration strategy prioritizes premium, seamless consumer experiences led by digital and owned stores, with continued investments in ERP, data/analytics, and end-to-end tech to drive speed, growth and efficiency.

- FY2023 financial highlights: Record revenues of $51.2B (+10% reported, +16% currency-neutral). NIKE Direct revenues rose to $21.3B (44% of NIKE Brand). Gross margin declined 250 bps to 43.5% due to higher product/input/freight costs, elevated promotions, and FX headwinds, partly offset by strategic pricing. Inventories were $8.5B (flat YoY). $7.5B returned to shareholders (buybacks/dividends). ROIC 31.5% (down from 46.5%).

- Market conditions: Demand remained strong despite macro uncertainty. Inflation pressured margins; supply chain volatility and COVID-related disruptions (notably in Greater China early in the year) normalized by Q4 FY23. Significant FX headwinds reduced reported revenue growth and pre-tax income. Ongoing macro risks could affect FY2024 growth and profitability.

- Recent developments: Transition to a distributor model in Central and South America (Chile, Argentina, Uruguay) completed; expected to temper reported revenue growth (due to commercial terms) but improve profitability over time and reduce FX exposure.

- Non-GAAP metrics and key definitions: EBIT, EBIT margin, ROIC, currency-neutral revenue, wholesale equivalent revenue; comparable store sales definition and methodology.

- Consolidated results: Revenue $51.2B; cost of sales up 15%; net income $5.1B (-16%); diluted EPS $3.23 (-14%). NIKE Brand footwear +20% currency-neutral (units +13%, ASP +7 pts); apparel +8% currency-neutral (units +4%, ASP +4 pts). NIKE Direct +14% reported (+20% currency-neutral) with digital sales $12.6B (+24%) and comparable store sales +14%. Jordan Brand led growth (+35% currency-neutral on wholesale equivalent basis), with Men’s, Women’s, and Kids’ also up.

- Margin and expenses: Gross margin down 250 bps on higher product/input/freight costs, greater promotions, FX, and lower off-price margin; partially offset by higher full-price ASP and lower inventory obsolescence vs prior year in China. SG&A up 11%: demand creation +5% (advertising, sports marketing); operating overhead +12% (wages, NIKE Direct variable costs, tech investments).

- Other income/expense and taxes: Net other income increased, driven by favorable FX conversion effects and lapping prior-year Russia deconsolidation charge, partially offset by distributor transition losses in APLA. Effective tax rate rose to 18.2% (lower stock-comp benefits and prior-year one-time IP onshoring benefit). Inflation Reduction Act minimum tax not expected to be material.

- Segment performance:
  - North America: Revenue +18% currency-neutral; digital +23%; footwear +22%; EBIT +7%; gross margin -310 bps (costs, promotions).
  - EMEA: Revenue +21% currency-neutral; digital +43%; footwear +25%; EBIT +7%; gross margin -60 bps (costs, FX), partially offset by pricing/mix.
  - Greater China: Revenue +4% currency-neutral; comps +9%, digital -4%; footwear +8%; EBIT -3%; gross margin +140 bps (prior-year obsolescence, FX, pricing/mix), offset by higher input costs.
  - APLA: Revenue +17% currency-neutral (CASA distributor shift reduced growth by ~5 pts); Direct +22%; footwear +19%; EBIT +2%; gross margin -190 bps (costs, FX).
  - Global Brand Divisions: Higher loss on increased wage and enterprise technology investments.
  - Converse: Revenue +8% currency-neutral (strength in North America and Western Europe, weakness in Asia); ASP +6%; EBIT +1%; slight gross margin expansion.

- Corporate: Larger EBIT loss driven by higher corporate overhead and unfavorable variance between actual and standard FX rates (net of hedges); partially offset by favorable FX remeasurement in Other income.

- FX exposures and hedging: Detailed discussion of transactional exposures (product costs via NIKE Trading Company and factory currency index, non-functional currency sales, other costs, balance sheet items) and translational exposures; use of natural offsets and derivatives (forwards/options). Estimated FY23 FX impact on pre-tax income: -$1.023B.

- Liquidity and capital resources: Strong liquidity with $10.7B in cash and short-term investments; operating cash flow $5.8B (improved working capital), investing inflow from net redemptions of short-term investments, financing outflow $7.4B (buybacks, $500M debt maturity, lower option proceeds). Active shelf registration; $2B five-year and $1B 364-day credit facilities; $3B CP program (unused); investment-grade ratings. Material cash obligations include $7.6B endorsements ($1.3B within 12 months), $6.4B product purchase obligations (all within 12 months), $3.3B other purchase obligations ($1.7B within 12 months), and $644M transition tax payable ($161M within 12 months). No material off-balance sheet arrangements.

- Critical accounting estimates: Sales-related reserves (returns/discounts), inventory reserves (NRV), hedge accounting for derivatives, income tax estimates and uncertain tax positions, and legal contingencies. New accounting pronouncements referenced.

structure.title: Quantitative and Qualitative Disclosures about Market Risk
structure.heading: ITEM 7A. Quantitative and Qualitative Disclosures about Market Risk
structure.start_phrase: In the normal course of business and consistent with established policies and procedures, we employ a variety of financial instruments to manage exposure to fluctuations in the value of foreign currencies and interest rates.
structure.summary:
- Focus: Quantitative and qualitative disclosures about market risk, covering foreign currency and interest rate exposures, hedging strategies, and risk measurement.
- Policy: Uses financial instruments only to finance the business and manage risks; no trading or speculation.
- Foreign currency risk: Arises from international sales, sourcing, and funding. Hedged with forward and option contracts for anticipated and firm transactions and related receivables/payables (third-party and intercompany). Hedging can begin 12–24 months before forecasted transactions and may reach up to 100% of exposure by transaction date. Majority are designated as cash flow hedges, primarily for EUR/USD, GBP/EUR, CNY/USD, and JPY/USD. Hedging can delay exchange-rate impacts on financial statements. See Note 12 for details.
- Interest rate risk: Exposure to short- and long-term rate movements. Managed by maintaining a mix of commercial paper, bank loans, and fixed-rate debt with varying maturities to limit earnings/cash flow volatility and reduce borrowing costs.
- Market risk measurement: Uses market value review, sensitivity analysis, and Value-at-Risk (VaR). VaR (95% confidence, variance-covariance method) applies only to FX derivatives (forwards and options), with option sensitivities (delta/gamma) incorporated. VaR excludes impacts on underlying non-functional currency transactions and does not capture potential favorable rate moves or full loss extremes.
- VaR results: Estimated maximum one-day loss on FX derivatives was $111 million at May 31, 2023, vs. $99 million in 2022, driven by higher FX volatility; such derivative losses would be offset by gains in hedged exposures. Average monthly change in FX derivative fair values: $289 million (fiscal 2023) vs. $170 million (fiscal 2022).
- Items excluded from VaR: Intercompany loans in non-functional currencies and fixed-rate USD debt. Intercompany loans and interest are eliminated in consolidation and substantially hedged with forwards; related market risks considered immaterial.
- Debt profile: $9.0 billion of fixed-rate USD long-term debt outstanding, maturing $1.0 billion in 2025 (avg 2.4%), $2.0 billion in 2027 (avg 2.6%), and $6.0 billion thereafter (avg 3.3%); none in 2024, 2026, or 2028. Total fair value $7.889 billion; overall average interest rate 3.1%.

  - Derivatives recorded gross; collateral practices described.
  - Committed credit facilities: $2.0B five-year (matures 2027, extendable) and $1.0B 364-day (matures 2024, extendable); no borrowings outstanding at year-end.

- Income taxes (detail)
